Counterexample: “Both are grammar errors, so copy ten whole sentences” names neither target. A meaningful word-part explanation does not substitute for listening to a sound contrast; pronunciation repetition alone does not explain the prefix's contribution.

GUIDED PAUSE A — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED; NO INDEPENDENT ATTEMPT)
A learner can pronounce “unfair” but asks how it differs from “fair.” Which unit would you examine first? Feedback: the meaning of the prefix un- makes morphology a useful starting point. Check the whole sentence too: knowing a part is a resource for interpreting a word in context, not a guarantee that every similar-looking word works the same way. This static pause records no response, attempt, judgment or evidence. [S1; S5 word-part instruction]

STAGE 2 — BEGIN WITH THE FUNCTION, THEN CHOOSE FORMS
A function is what language accomplishes: informing, persuading, supporting an argument, comparing or sequencing. Forms are the resources used to do it. “Because,” “although,” a claim followed by evidence, and a sentence acknowledging a competing interpretation can help an argument. Time adverbs help order events, but a presentation's topic alone does not make sequencing its only useful function. The supplied S1 sample-family cue is not a universal key, and no published item is reproduced here. [S1]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — THE SAME EVIDENCE, TWO AUDIENCES
A class investigates whether a school courtyard should include a quiet reading area. For a partner conversation, a learner says, “I think the shaded corner works because our notes show people already read there.” In a written proposal to the facilities committee, the learner writes, “We recommend retaining a shaded reading area because the observations indicate existing use; however, the proposal must also preserve an accessible route.”
Reasoning: both versions support a claim. The committee version makes the recommendation and qualification more explicit for readers outside the class. Discourse connects the claim, evidence and limitation; sentence forms express reason and concession; words such as “recommend” add precision. The authored forms are possibilities, not the only correct register. Changing audience does not establish a personality trait or require erasing a learner's voice. [S1/S2]
Counterexample: replacing the argument with “First, next, finally” may order points, but it does not by itself connect evidence to a recommendation or address the competing need. Requiring informal conversation to sound like a formal letter also ignores context.

GUIDED PAUSE B — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED)
Suggest one question that would improve the proposal and one form that could express its answer. Feedback: “What might change our recommendation?” invites a limitation; “Although …, we recommend … because …” can make the tradeoff visible. Other forms work if they serve the intended function. The goal is reasoned communication, not counting connectors. No response or success is stored. [S1/S2]

STAGE 3 — USE CROSS-LANGUAGE RESOURCES WITH CHECKS
Transfer means that knowledge or patterns from one language can influence another. Familiar literacy strategies or a verified true cognate can help. A sound or syntax pattern may also produce a mismatch in the new context; a false cognate can suggest an incorrect meaning. These possibilities do not establish the cause of any particular learner's response. Languages differ, and not all languages offer the same cognate connections with English. S5 illustrates investigación/investigation as a useful connection and directs teachers to check false cognates, context and word parts. [S1/S5]
L1 academic language and literacy are resources: S9 quotes WIDA on academic development in one language facilitating development in the other. This does not mean all transfer is positive, every language pair shares cognates, or a learner must abandon a familiar language to develop English. S3 also values learners' full linguistic repertoires. [S3/S9]

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — VERIFY THE CONNECTION
In a synthetic research project, a learner knows investigación. Linking it to “investigation,” using both in a meaningful research question, and checking the learner's explanation can unlock the English word. For a different word, the class's trusted bilingual reference explicitly shows that the similar-looking familiar-language word has a different meaning. Teach that contrast in two sentences instead of accepting the resemblance as proof.
Reasoning: the decision rule is verification, not visual similarity. Keep the useful connection in the first situation and explain the misleading connection in the second. Rejecting all familiar-language resources because one connection misleads would discard assets. The false-friend situation supplies the contrast as a synthetic fact; it does not make an unsupported claim about a named language pair. [S5/S3]

GUIDED PAUSE C — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED)
A colleague proposes the same English-cognate list for every language background. Feedback: S5 cautions that not all languages lend themselves to those cross-language connections. Ask which languages and words actually connect, verify meanings, and offer context, visuals and word-part reasoning when cognates do not help. No learner label or language background establishes ability. No attempt or independent evidence is created. [S5]

REMAINING GAPS AND NEXT STEPS
The four statements remain partial: this lesson does not teach a full phonological inventory, comprehensive morphology or syntax, all rhetorical registers and writing conventions, the Massachusetts ELA framework in detail, or systematic contrasts across language pairs. It makes no cognate-utility percentages or causal claim about an individual's error. The linked unaided checks sample separate decisions; set aside this assistance and record any help through existing practice controls. The unfamiliar audience-and-argument case requires analysis, uncertainty and justification and remains provisional/manual. Its tag alone proves no transfer. Native cards are recall supports only. Mapping, instruction, model review and independent learner evidence remain distinct.

lessons.title: Language profiles and learning environments: support access without labels
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE — PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0005

This original instruction samples the six existing Objective 0005 statements. Synthetic profiles illustrate planning; they are not individual diagnoses, official test items or placement rules. Source labels identify the user-supplied packet, independently retrieved by its researcher on 2026-11-08, America/New_York. Codex did not retrieve the documents. Model comparison is not human review.

These assisted guided checks create no attempts or independent evidence.

LEARNING GOALS
Content goal: interpret a domain-specific language observation, reject an unsupported high-stakes inference, and plan a rigorous learning opportunity whose language support responds to observed performance and context.
Language goal: state a bounded interpretation with “in this task/domain at this time …,” propose a support with “because …,” and identify uncertainty with “we would need further evidence about ….” Explain why an alternative plan would lose information or reduce access.

STAGE 1 — USE THEORIES AS PLANNING QUESTIONS
Social and academic language distinguish demands of situations, not two fixed types of learners. Successful everyday conversation does not establish control of the language needed to compare sources, qualify a claim or explain a disciplinary relationship. Conversely, a learner may have academic knowledge and literacy in a familiar language while developing English resources to express it. S1 names these planning concepts; S9 quotes WIDA that academic development in a native language facilitates academic development in English and that the relationship also works in the other direction. [S1/S9]
Interdependence or “dual iceberg” is used here only as a planning construct for drawing on shared academic knowledge and literacy resources. No iceberg diagram, full Cummins theory or universal BICS/CALP year counts are supplied. Do not predict a learner's acquisition timeline. Transfer may help or interfere depending on the resource and context; the previous lesson checks both. [S1/S9]

STAGE 2 — DESCRIBE LANGUAGE PERFORMANCE, NOT THE PERSON
The exam inventory names entering, emerging, developing, expanding, bridging and reaching. Those level names are not cognitive ranks, readiness categories or permanent identities. WIDA PLDs describe snapshots of language use in a domain at a point in time. Say “a student's writing performance in this task is described at PL2,” not “a Level 2 student.” A learner may speak at a higher proficiency level while writing at an earlier level; the evidence and domain must travel with the description. [S1/S2]
Listening, speaking, reading and writing remain useful domains for planning. WIDA 2020 also uses interpretive modes, including listening, reading and viewing, and expressive modes, including speaking, writing and representing. “Expressive” is not synonymous with only speaking. Development is non-linear and contingent on topic, audience and situation; a change in task performance is not proof of a permanent regression. [S2]
Can Do Descriptors provide examples of language use in situations and content areas. They supplement standards; they do not replace standards or the 2020 Language Expectations. S10 notes they have not yet been updated to the 2020 Edition. Use that version caution explicitly rather than claiming the documents are interchangeable. [S4/S10]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — AN UNEVEN PROFILE IN A HISTORY INQUIRY
In a synthetic grade 7 inquiry, Mina gives an extended spoken explanation about an artifact after familiar-language planning. Her independent English paragraph names two details but does not yet link them to a claim. A recent classroom observation describes stronger speaking than writing; reading evidence is incomplete.
Reasoning: retain the demanding task of comparing interpretations of the artifact. Offer access to the complex source with images, purposeful chunking and discussion, then model how a detail supports a claim. Let Mina rehearse an explanation before writing, and inspect what changes when support is reduced. Record the domain, task, context and assistance. Do not assume reading performance from speaking, or assign a single global level from this account. These are authored planning options consistent with S2's domain distinctions and access protections, not a prescription keyed to a level. [S2/S7]
Counterexample: replacing the inquiry with copying simple labels because writing is emerging confuses language performance with cognitive ability and removes evidence reasoning. PLDs must not limit complex texts, grade-level materials, rigorous learning or meaningful discussion. [S2]

GUIDED PAUSE A — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED; NO INDEPENDENT ATTEMPT)
What can the profile justify, and what remains unknown? Feedback: it supports investigating how oral planning and explicit evidence-linking help this writing task; it does not establish reading ability, disability or a permanent level. A later independent sample can inform teaching, but reading this example creates no attempt, judgment or evidence. [S2]

STAGE 3 — SEPARATE INFLUENCES FROM DESTINY
S1 lists physical, cognitive, educational, affective and sociocultural influences. Prior schooling, literacy resources, continuity of opportunity, metalinguistic awareness, motivation, inhibition, identity and classroom relationships can shape rate and pathway. None alone determines outcomes, and this packet provides no causal ranking. S3 emphasizes individual experiences, meaningful engagement and the full linguistic repertoire. Investigate available opportunities and the individual's observed strategies; do not infer ability, disability, trauma, nationality traits or culture-based learning types from language background. [S1/S3]
An inquiry about sociocultural opportunity might ask whether classroom routines value a learner's languages or make participation risky. It does not assign “social distance” or cultural identity from a name or nationality. Broader political and ideological mechanisms remain a gap. A quieter response on an unfamiliar topic could reflect task knowledge, audience, language demands or another circumstance; seek evidence instead of choosing a single cause. [S1/S2/S3]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — A CHANGED TOPIC AND AN UNHELPFUL INTERPRETATION
After confident discussion of a familiar story, a learner contributes shorter responses in a new unit about municipal archives before an unfamiliar audience. A colleague says the learner has “gone down a level forever.”
Reasoning: S2 explicitly makes development non-linear and contingent on topic, audience and situation. Compare the demands and supports, invite preparation with the source, and observe performance across further opportunities. The changed sample supplies information for instruction; it is not a permanent identity or a schedule of how long development must take. L1 reading strategies may help locate evidence without implying that every language feature transfers directly. [S2/S9]
Counterexample: setting a fixed social-language/academic-language clock would replace observation with a timeline the packet does not support.

GUIDED PAUSE B — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED)
A team proposes special education placement solely from an English proficiency level. Feedback: S2 lists that use as inapplicable. PLDs must not be sole evidence for special education, cognitive ability or readiness descriptions, tracking, report-card grading or grade placement/retention. Seek the appropriate wider evidence and process; this lesson supplies no eligibility rule. Rejecting the inference does not predetermine whether a learner has a disability. No guided answer is stored. [S2]

STAGE 4 — REDUCE PARTICIPATION RISK WHILE KEEPING THE REASONING
A predictable routine, a visual anchor, rehearsal with a partner and explicit invitation to ask for clarification can make purposeful communication more accessible. These authored choices illustrate S1's supportive-environment scope and S7's rigorous, purposefully scaffolded learning. The affective-filter construct is not permission to remove demanding ideas or to infer someone's inner state. Calibrate feedback to purpose: during a first attempt to explain a claim, attend to meaning and a selected useful prompt; during a later focused practice on an evidence-linking form, make that form explicit. Neither constant interruption nor “never correct anything” follows from the packet. [S1/S7]

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — CONTENT LANGUAGE AND DEDICATED ESL
A science class is comparing competing explanations. A schedule proposal removes multilingual learners from that core lesson for unrelated word copying and says only the ESL teacher teaches language.
Reasoning: S7 describes academic language development across content lessons and dedicated ESL time that attends closely to language practices and skill areas. Preserve core SEI content instruction and coordinate the dedicated ESL focus; students can practice justifying conclusions in both contexts. This is a bounded program distinction, not a new scheduling mandate or invented service-minute rule. [S7]
Counterexample: keeping the class but removing the comparison goal also loses rigor. Meaningful access needs both content reasoning and intentional language support.

GUIDED PAUSE C — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED)
A student hesitates during an initial argument rehearsal. Choose one participation support and one later feedback focus. Feedback: previewing the source with a partner can support a first attempt; later examine how “because” connects evidence to the claim. Other choices need a task-based reason. Do not infer low motivation or a fixed cultural style from hesitation. No attempts or independent evidence are created. [S1/S7]

REMAINING GAPS AND NEXT STEPS
Coverage remains partial across all six statements. Full SLA theory, validated level-by-level instructional progressions, cognitive/physical causal mechanisms, comparative rates, broader sociopolitical analysis, assessment administration, placement/eligibility rules and district cut scores are not taught. Learning-styles matching is not a Field 56 requirement and has no supporting research excerpt here; no VARK-based plan is prescribed. The linked unaided checks sample bounded decisions; assistance must be recorded. The unfamiliar museum-profile case remains provisional/manual and requires a reasoned plan with uncertainty. A tag, lesson view, card review or model comparison is not independent evidence or objective completion.

lessons.title: Vocabulary, listening and talk across a content unit
lessons.body:
ORIGINAL UNOFFICIAL LEARNING MODULE — PARTIAL OBJECTIVE 0006

This original module samples the six existing Objective 0006 statements using synthetic K–8 content lessons. It is not an official examination item, a required word list or a complete oral-language curriculum. Source labels refer to the supplied packet; its researcher retrieved the material on 2026-11-08, America/New_York. Codex did not fetch it. Model comparison is not human review.

These assisted guided checks create no attempts or independent evidence.

LEARNING GOALS
Content goal: select a small set of useful words for a specific content text, justify the selection through meaning and language demands, and plan repeated word use with purposeful listening, speaking and writing.
Language goal: paraphrase a partner's main idea and one supporting detail, ask a clarification question, and use a selected word to justify a content claim. Explain a word choice with “in this context … means … because ….” These goals describe observable practice, not proficiency cutoffs.

STAGE 1 — CONNECT WORD LEARNING TO CONTENT AND EVIDENCE
The April 2014 IES/WWC practice guide addresses English-medium academic instruction in elementary and middle school, K–8. Recommendation 1 is intensive teaching of a set of academic vocabulary words across several days using varied activities. Recommendation 2 integrates oral and written English language instruction into content-area teaching. Both are rated Strong; the packet specifically identifies content-acquisition measures for Recommendation 2. These are evidence ratings within that guide, not invented effect sizes or a guarantee for an individual lesson. Pre-K and high-school applications require a scope caveat and additional evidence; this module's worked plans stay in K–8. [S5]
Academic vocabulary includes general academic and domain-specific vocabulary. Selection should serve the meaning of the actual lesson. The “three tiers” phrase appears in the exam inventory, but the Beck monograph was not supplied: this module invents no tier membership rules, official tier word lists or equation between tiers and WIDA proficiency levels. [S1/S5]

STAGE 2 — CHOOSE A FEW WORDS FOR A REASON
Ask which words unlock an important concept, which recur in the unit's reasoning, and what may make them challenging. A word may have multiple meanings, a useful or misleading cross-language resemblance, meaningful parts, or an idiomatic use. Teach the concept and contextual use, not only an isolated synonym. Not every familiar language supplies useful English cognates; verify proposed connections. S5 names word parts, cognates, false cognates and idiomatic extensions as relevant considerations. [S5]

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — A GRADE 6 COMMUNITY-GARDEN UNIT
Learners compare two original proposals for a school garden using observations of shade and access. The teacher selects “evidence,” “access” and “reusable” as an authored small set for this particular text, not a prescribed tier list. “Evidence” helps connect a recommendation to observations; “access” names whether people can reach and use the space; “reusable” can be examined through its meaningful parts and the idea of using material again.
Day 1: connect each word to a visual or concrete example and a contrasting nonexample in the text. Learners explain what makes an observation evidence for a particular claim.
Day 2: partners revisit the proposals, use the words to compare choices and paraphrase one another before responding. An accessible bilingual resource may verify a proposed cognate; a connection is used only if it fits the meaning.
Day 3: groups revise a recommendation after a new observation, then write a short justification using appropriate words. Later revisit the words in another relevant passage and inspect understanding beyond copied definitions.
Reasoning: repeated, varied use across days connects concept, talk and writing. The exact three-day design and selected words are authored illustrations of S5, not the only valid duration or list. A one-day dictionary-copying exercise would provide neither intensive varied use nor evidence of meaning in the unit. [S5/S6]

GUIDED PAUSE A — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED; NO INDEPENDENT ATTEMPT)
Why might the teacher omit a rare decorative word from this unit's intensive set? Feedback: prioritize words that help learners understand and communicate the unit's ideas, while explaining other words as needed. The decision is tied to the text and task, not a made-up tier rule. Copying a definition does not by itself show contextual understanding. This static guided pause stores no response, attempt, judgment or evidence. [S5]

STAGE 3 — LISTEN FOR MEANING, THEN USE IT
Oral work needs a purpose beyond taking turns. A listener can identify a main idea, note a supporting detail, paraphrase the speaker's reasoning and ask what evidence supports it. The speaker can clarify and revise. Then writing can preserve or extend the reasoning. These authored routines illustrate S1's listening/oral/literacy connections and S5/S6's integration of language with content; they are not a new scored speaking rubric. [S1/S5/S6]
Use a visual or organizer to anchor the content, but keep the task's intellectual demand. A simple language frame may support a complex comparison without supplying its answer. S3 includes oral, written, visual and kinesthetic modes as resources. Offering multiple modalities does not assign a permanent “visual learner” type. Feedback should focus on the intended meaning and language function; a first rehearsal and a focused revision can call for different kinds of correction. [S1/S3/S7]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — DAILY STRUCTURED TALK IN A HISTORY UNIT
A grade 5 class compares two accounts of how a neighborhood public space changed. Each pair has an image and an excerpt. Speaker A states an interpretation and a detail; Listener B paraphrases the interpretation, checks the detail against the source and asks one clarification question. They switch roles with the other account, then write one point of agreement and one unresolved question.
Reasoning: listening has an observable purpose, each speaker must respond to meaning, and writing uses the discussion. The teacher can notice whether a learner understood the main claim even if a sentence form still needs support. A short model of “I heard …; which detail supports …?” may help access; it is not a requirement to count exact phrases. [S1/S5/S6]
Counterexample: displaying word posters while students work silently all week does not implement daily opportunities to talk about content. Unstructured “chat if finished” also gives no clear listening target or reason to use the words.

GUIDED PAUSE B — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED)
A listener repeats a word from the speaker but cannot explain the claim. What next step fits the goal? Feedback: return to the source and ask for a paraphrase of the main idea and a relevant detail, with a model or visual if needed. More repetitions of the isolated word may not address listening comprehension. Accept varied wording that conveys the meaning; do not confuse exact phrase imitation with understanding. No independent evidence is created. [S1/S5/S6]

STAGE 4 — MAKE MEANING CHANGES VISIBLE
Polysemous words have multiple meanings, and different disciplines may use the same word differently. Teach the relevant meanings in their actual contexts. In an authored civics passage, “measure” may mean a proposed action or rule; in a science procedure, “measure” may describe determining a quantity. A learner who knows one use may need explicit comparison for the other. This illustrates the supplied S1 polysemy cue and S5's attention to multiple meanings; it is not an official test item. [S1/S5]

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — RESOURCES THAT HELP, RESOURCES THAT MISLEAD
A grade 7 inquiry text uses “investigation.” A learner already knows investigación, the connection supplied in S5. Verify the meaning in the inquiry sentence and invite the learner to use it to explain what is being investigated. Another proposed connection only looks similar; the class's reference explicitly identifies a different meaning. Contrast the meanings in context rather than banning all cross-language discussion. For “reusable,” examine re- and the whole word in the unit; do not teach that every word beginning with those letters has that prefix.
Reasoning: cognate, false-cognate, polysemy and morphology decisions ask different questions. Similar appearance is not proof, one familiar meaning is not every meaning, and word-part knowledge must be checked against context. No utility percentage or fixed language-group trait follows from these examples. [S5]

GUIDED PAUSE C — THINK, THEN COMPARE (ASSISTED)
A colleague says “measure” must be a rare technical Tier 3 word in every subject. Feedback: compare the two actual sentences and meanings. The packet supports contextual polysemy instruction, not that universal tier assignment. Create a small meaning map with examples as an authored option; do not claim that the packet validates every semantic-map, word-wall, drama, chant or technology method. No response or success is stored. [S1/S5]

REMAINING GAPS AND NEXT STEPS
The six statements remain partial. Full listening progressions, all oral/interpersonal skills, the WIDA Speaking Rubric and Massachusetts ELA details, achievement effect sizes, tier taxonomy, comprehensive idiom instruction, and evaluations of particular vocabulary technologies or activity formats are gaps. S5's K–8 scope must travel with its claims. The linked unaided checks sample distinct decisions. The unfamiliar civic-unit case requires a multi-day plan, justified word choices, listening/talk/writing and uncertainty; it has no deterministic answer key and remains provisional/manual. An unfamiliar tag proves no transfer. Native flashcards support recall only; neither cards, guided pauses nor lesson reading create independent evidence or complete an objective.

tasks.title: What does the survey establish?
tasks.prompt: A new student’s Language Survey reports a language other than English. Which conclusion is justified by that information alone?

options.text: The student must have weak mathematics knowledge.
The information belongs in the district’s process for deciding whether proficiency screening is needed.
The student has already received an English proficiency score.

answerKey.feedback: The survey provides language-background information; the authorized identification process and proficiency evidence determine status. It does not measure mathematical ability.

wrongFeedback.a: Language background does not measure content knowledge. Separate the constructs.
wrongFeedback.c: A survey response is not a proficiency assessment result.

tasks.title: Separate family communication from identification
tasks.prompt: A parent requests translated written communication. No student proficiency evidence is available. What should a teacher infer?

options.text: The child is automatically an EL.
The parent request can be ignored if the child speaks English.
Honor the communication need and use the appropriate identification evidence for the child.

answerKey.feedback: The protocol separates family communication preferences from identification questions. A family’s language-access needs and a child’s proficiency are related contexts, not interchangeable measures.

wrongFeedback.a: A parent’s communication preference alone does not establish the child’s EL status.
wrongFeedback.b: Family communication needs do not disappear because a child speaks English.

tasks.title: Name the distinction
tasks.prompt: In a few words, name what must be assessed separately from language-background survey information to determine English-language proficiency.

answerKey.feedback: Look for direct evidence of English proficiency through the appropriate assessment process. Longer or differently phrased answers need review rather than an automatic incorrect label.

tasks.title: Who plans access?
tasks.prompt: An algebra teacher says only the ESL teacher should adapt access to algebra discussions. Which response best fits shared responsibility?

options.text: Keep the algebra goal and coordinate content-language supports with the ESL colleague.
Wait for fluent English before teaching algebra.
Remove discussion and give only computation.

answerKey.feedback: The content teacher plans access to content and academic discourse while coordinating specialist expertise.

wrongFeedback.b: Waiting withholds content access instead of planning support.
wrongFeedback.c: Removing reasoning/discussion changes the target and avoids the language-development need.

tasks.title: Bring useful evidence to a team
tasks.prompt: Which note best supports shared planning after a ratio lesson?

options.text: Needs ESL; no further details.
Explained equivalent ratios with a diagram; needed a frame to connect the explanation in writing.
Has an accent, so does not understand ratios.

answerKey.feedback: Specific evidence identifies content understanding, the language domain, and assistance. It lets colleagues choose a next step.

wrongFeedback.a: A label without task evidence gives colleagues little basis for planning.
wrongFeedback.c: Accent is not evidence of mathematical misunderstanding.

tasks.title: Recall the responsibility
tasks.prompt: Who shares responsibility for educating and supporting English learners? Give the broad group, not only one specialist role.

answerKey.feedback: All educators share responsibility. This does not erase specialized roles or individual support plans.

tasks.title: Respond to evidence after exit
tasks.prompt: A former EL understands a graph but struggles to write its explanation. What is the best classroom response?

options.text: Ignore the difficulty because the student is a former EL.
Automatically change the student’s official status based on this answer.
Provide evidence-based academic-language support and share observations through the appropriate team.

answerKey.feedback: Support the observed need and use the established team/process for status decisions. One classroom response is not a reclassification rule.

wrongFeedback.a: A status label does not remove an instructional need.
wrongFeedback.b: A single classroom answer does not replace current official criteria and procedures.

tasks.title: Find the authority for a policy claim
tasks.prompt: A study card states an exit threshold using a historical framework reference alone. What should happen before it is taught as current Massachusetts policy?

options.text: Use the old reference because all published rules stay unchanged.
Compare the claim with current official guidance, record version/effective-date limits, and leave a gap if unresolved.
Use whichever threshold sounds reasonable.

answerKey.feedback: Framework references identify topics to study. Current operational rules require current authoritative evidence, not historical mentions or plausibility.

wrongFeedback.a: A historical reference can become outdated.
wrongFeedback.c: A plausible number is not legal or policy evidence.

tasks.title: Name the policy gap
tasks.prompt: A numeric exit threshold has no current official verification. What should this app call it? Answer with the gap label.

answerKey.feedback: Keep it a policy-research gap. Do not infer a legal rule from a classroom example.

tasks.title: Conversation and explanation
tasks.prompt: A student chats comfortably but struggles to justify a comparison of two rates. Which interpretation supports instruction?

options.text: Social fluency does not guarantee control of the academic language of justification.
Comfortable conversation proves the student is avoiding work.
The student cannot understand rates.

answerKey.feedback: Analyze the language function and task evidence. Teach the comparison and justification language alongside the content.

wrongFeedback.b: Conversation alone is not evidence of motivation or avoidance.
wrongFeedback.c: Difficulty expressing a justification does not by itself establish lack of content understanding.

tasks.title: Beyond a word list
tasks.prompt: Students know rate and constant but cannot connect a claim to supporting values. Which support targets the missing demand most directly?

options.text: Ask them to copy the vocabulary definitions again.
Reduce the task to circling a number.
Model a connected explanation and have them rehearse a claim-evidence connection using their own values.

answerKey.feedback: The barrier includes sentence/discourse relationships. A word list alone does not teach how to connect evidence and a claim.

wrongFeedback.a: The evidence points beyond isolated word meaning.
wrongFeedback.b: Circling a number removes the explanation target.

tasks.title: Recall the language category
tasks.prompt: What kind of language is used to explain, argue, and justify ideas within school subjects? Use the two-word category.

answerKey.feedback: Academic language includes word/phrase, sentence, and discourse demands; it is more than technical vocabulary.

tasks.title: Read the profile
tasks.prompt: Two learners have the same overall English proficiency result. One has stronger speaking and weaker writing. What should planning do?

options.text: Give both learners identical supports solely from the overall result.
Use domain evidence and classroom work to tailor supports while retaining content goals.
Assume stronger speaking means writing no longer needs instruction.

answerKey.feedback: A composite can hide differences among listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Use disaggregated evidence and the actual task.

wrongFeedback.a: An overall result does not describe each domain equally.
wrongFeedback.c: Speaking can support writing, but it does not replace writing development.

tasks.title: Match evidence to a domain
tasks.prompt: A student follows an oral explanation and gives a clear spoken response but struggles to interpret a written prompt. Which next step is most defensible?

options.text: Treat the oral evidence as proof of identical reading proficiency.
Stop collecting domain evidence.
Investigate the reading demand and plan a support, using the oral strengths as resources.

answerKey.feedback: The observations concern different domains. Investigate text demands instead of collapsing them into one label.

wrongFeedback.a: Evidence in listening/speaking does not establish the same performance in reading.
wrongFeedback.b: More precise evidence helps target instruction; less evidence does not.

tasks.title: Retrieve the missing domain
tasks.prompt: Name the fourth language domain: listening, speaking, reading, and ____.

answerKey.feedback: Writing is a distinct domain. This narrow recall check alone cannot demonstrate good instructional planning.

tasks.title: Score the intended construct
tasks.prompt: A learner’s diagram and reasoning correctly show why two ratios are equivalent, but the written explanation has article errors. If the target is proportional reasoning, what is appropriate?

options.text: Score all reasoning as incorrect because the English is imperfect.
Recognize the mathematical evidence and give separate language feedback.
Treat fluent grammar as the only evidence needed.

answerKey.feedback: Judge evidence relevant to the content target and separate language feedback. Neither grammatical accuracy nor inaccuracy alone establishes mathematical understanding.

wrongFeedback.a: Article errors do not erase valid mathematical evidence.
wrongFeedback.c: Fluent grammar can accompany incorrect mathematics.

tasks.title: Purpose before format
tasks.prompt: A teacher uses an exit ticket to decide which representation to model tomorrow. What makes this a formative use?

options.text: It informs the next instructional decision.
It is automatically formative because it contains only one question.
It produces an official English proficiency classification.

answerKey.feedback: Formative use concerns evidence used to adjust teaching/learning. Format or length alone does not determine purpose.

wrongFeedback.b: A short item can serve different purposes; identify the use.
wrongFeedback.c: A classroom exit ticket does not replace the official identification process.

tasks.title: Retrieve the assessment purpose
tasks.prompt: What is the usual label for assessment used during learning to guide the next teaching and learning steps?

answerKey.feedback: Formative assessment informs action during learning; summative use summarizes achievement. Task format alone does not decide the purpose.

tasks.title: Use an oral strength
tasks.prompt: A learner explains a linear relationship orally but writes only fragments. Which sequence best develops writing?

options.text: Replace all future writing with speech.
Require silent writing with no connection to the demonstrated oral strength.
Rehearse the explanation, notice a modeled written structure, then write and review with support.

answerKey.feedback: Use oral strength as a bridge and retain an explicit writing goal. Adjust support from evidence.

wrongFeedback.a: Permanent substitution avoids the writing-development goal.
wrongFeedback.b: Removing a useful scaffold needlessly ignores the learner’s demonstrated strength.

tasks.title: Check what transferred
tasks.prompt: After rehearsing with a partner, students write a comparison. Which evidence best informs the next step?

options.text: Whether the writing connects the student’s claim to relevant data, and which language support was used.
Whether everyone spoke for exactly the same number of seconds.
Whether the paragraph is long, regardless of reasoning.

answerKey.feedback: Inspect the intended content-language relation and assistance. Duration and length alone do not establish a successful explanation.

wrongFeedback.b: Speaking time alone does not show what transferred to writing.
wrongFeedback.c: Length alone does not establish accuracy or reasoning.

tasks.title: Retrieve the intermediate step
tasks.prompt: What two-word strategy lets a student try out an explanation aloud before writing?

answerKey.feedback: Oral rehearsal can help organize meaning and language before a distinct written attempt.

tasks.title: Choose a scaffold
tasks.prompt: The goal is to compare rates and justify a decision. Which change best preserves that goal?

options.text: Replace comparison with copying multiplication facts.
Offer a labeled graph and optional comparison frame while students choose and justify the better rate.
Give the complete decision and have students copy it.

answerKey.feedback: The scaffold improves access while leaving comparison, evidence selection, and justification to the learner.

wrongFeedback.a: The replacement task changes the intellectual objective.
wrongFeedback.c: Copying the complete answer removes the evidence of independent reasoning.

tasks.title: Decide when to adjust a scaffold
tasks.prompt: A student uses a comparison frame accurately. What is the most informative next step?

options.text: Remove all supports permanently after one success.
Keep the identical frame forever without checking independence.
Try a suitable task with less support, record assistance, and use the evidence to adjust.

answerKey.feedback: Scaffolding responds to evidence and builds independence. One assisted success is not independent mastery.

wrongFeedback.a: One supported success may not transfer to unsupported work.
wrongFeedback.b: Permanent unchanged support prevents an honest check of independence.

tasks.title: Retrieve the support concept
tasks.prompt: What is the term for temporary, responsive instructional support that helps a learner work toward a demanding goal?

answerKey.feedback: A scaffold changes access and support while preserving the intended intellectual work; it should respond to evidence.

tasks.title: Case: a new student and a premature label
tasks.prompt:
Authored unfamiliar application. A new grade 9 learner uses two languages at home, solves a visual proportion problem, and hesitates during an English explanation. A colleague wants to assign EL status from the home-language information and move the student to easier mathematics.

1. Separate what each observation does and does not establish.
2. Identify the appropriate next step for English-proficiency determination without inventing a threshold.

tasks.title: Build the initial identification evidence chain
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check. A newly enrolling child has no documented prior EL/FEL determination. After clarification with the family, the June 2025 Language Survey rubric indicates that screening is needed. A teacher observes very little English during an informal conversation. Which next-action sequence is supported?

options.text: Use the informal conversation to determine EL status, start a placement, and administer the screener later to confirm it.
Treat the survey's other-language information as the proficiency result, determine EL status, and document placement.
Complete and score the indicated ELP screening, use results for determination and initial placement, then notify the family and document the decisions.
Use success in a supported content lesson to decide whether the indicated screener can be omitted.

answerKey.feedback: The protocol determines whether screening is indicated; when it is needed for initial identification, screening results support determination and placement. Notice and recording the determination/placement follow. The scenario supplies no transfer exception and no cut score. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08; S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08; S2 source.obj0001.s2.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: An impression of very little English does not justify initial placement before required screening. The S5 FAQ explicitly rejects that shortcut. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: A Language Survey is background information interpreted through the protocol, not an English proficiency result or automatic classification. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08; S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Content success does not replace the ELP screening indicated in this scenario. Use the required language evidence; do not invent an exception from a classroom observation. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08; S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Interpret Section 2 for family communication
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check. A family's Language Survey Section 2 requests interpreted meetings and translated messages. A staff member wants to use that request as evidence that the child needs EL placement. Which correction best fits the supplied protocol?

options.text: Use Section 2 to support family communication access; determine the child's identification needs from the appropriate child information and protocol.
Use the family's preferred language as the child's screening result when the parent cannot explain the child's English proficiency.
Postpone responding to the communication preference until the child's EL determination is complete.
Treat Section 2 as an additional identification question that overrides the Section 1 rubric.

answerKey.feedback: Section 2 is informational and is not used to identify whether the child needs support learning English. Family communication access and child identification need separate attention. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08; S6 source.obj0001.s6.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: A parent's language preference is neither the child's proficiency nor a screening result. Preserve the distinction between family access and child identification evidence. [S6 source.obj0001.s6.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Section 2's communication purpose does not depend on establishing the child's EL status. It can inform family communication while child identification follows its own process. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08; S6 source.obj0001.s6.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: The form expressly excludes Section 2 from child identification. It does not override the Section 1 protocol or rubric. [S5 source.obj0001.s5.2026-11-08; S6 source.obj0001.s6.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Coordinate content access and ESL
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check. An identified EL receives ESL instruction and participates in a science investigation. A scheduling conflict leads a team to propose replacing ESL with a sheltered science worksheet. The parent has not declined services. Which plan best fits shared responsibility?

options.text: Count the sheltered worksheet as ESL because it includes vocabulary and the student remains in a content classroom.
Have content and ESL teachers coordinate language support and observations while preserving ESL instruction and access to the science goal.
Assign language development exclusively to the ESL teacher and remove language scaffolds from science to avoid duplication.
Recommend that the parent decline ESL so the science timetable can remain unchanged.

answerKey.feedback: Language development is shared across content and ESL settings, but sheltering content is not a substitute for ESL. A scheduling problem does not justify recommending that a parent decline services. Voluntary informed parent opt-out is a separate matter. [S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08; S8 source.obj0001.s8.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: A useful content scaffold does not become ESL instruction by including vocabulary. S7 explicitly rejects sheltering as a substitute for ESL. [S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Shared responsibility includes content classrooms. Specialist expertise does not remove the content teacher's responsibility to support language access. [S1 source.obj0001.s1.2026-11-08; S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: The S8 changes summary says districts must not recommend declining services to resolve scheduling issues. Parent choice must remain separate from a timetable workaround. [S8 source.obj0001.s8.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Complete determination and placement communication
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check. A district has made a student's EL determination and program placement decision through the appropriate process. Its record currently contains only the screener result. Which completion action matches the supplied 603 CMR 14.02 duty? No notification deadline is being tested.

options.text: Retain the screener result alone because the determination and placement can be inferred from its score.
Tell the classroom teacher the placement; notify the parent only if the parent asks for an explanation.
Notify the parent of the determination but record only placement, since the two decisions refer to the same student.
Notify the parent or guardian of both the EL determination and program placement, and place both in the student's school record.

answerKey.feedback: 603 CMR 14.02(3) names both the EL determination and program placement for parent/guardian notification and the student's school record. A screening result alone does not state both decisions. No different notification clocks are combined here. [S2 source.obj0001.s2.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: The regulation requires recording the determination and placement, not relying on a reader to infer them from a screener result. [S2 source.obj0001.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Internal teacher communication does not replace the named parent/guardian notification duty. It is not conditional on a parent request. [S2 source.obj0001.s2.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: The duty covers both decisions in both places: parent notification and the student record. Splitting the information leaves the stated duty incomplete. [S2 source.obj0001.s2.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Retrieve the status after voluntary opt-out
tasks.prompt: Original unaided finite recall. An identified EL's parent voluntarily declines ELE services. No reclassification has occurred. What status does the student retain? Respond with only the status label or acronym; explanations beyond this finite key need review.

answerKey.feedback: The student remains an English Learner (EL). Opt-out is a service choice, not reclassification or FEL status. January 2026 guidance says annual English proficiency testing (WIDA ACCESS) continues. Shared responsibility for learning access also continues; this answer does not establish any exit criterion. Other wording or nuanced explanations remain pending review. [S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08; S1 source.obj0001.s1.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Continue support for a documented FEL
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check. A student registers with documented FEL status and is still within the four-year monitoring period after reclassification described by January 2026 guidance (supplied retrieval 2026-11-08). The student explains a historical image well but struggles to connect evidence in writing. Which response is supported by the supplied excerpts?

options.text: Treat the writing difficulty as sufficient evidence to change the student's official status back to EL.
Provide no language-related support because reclassification establishes that all later academic language demands are secure.
Recognize the documented FEL status, continue routine academic-progress monitoring and respond to the observed need without restarting the period or inferring a status change.
Begin a new four-year period at registration, because monitoring belongs only to the district that currently enrolls the student.

answerKey.feedback: January 2026 guidance, supplied retrieval 2026-11-08, requires identifying FELs on registration and routine academic-progress monitoring for four years after reclassification; S8 corroborates the duration. A transfer is not a new reclassification event. Support the observed need; the excerpts do not supply a complete monitoring schedule or a rule for automatic status change. [S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08; S8 source.obj0001.s8.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: A classroom difficulty calls for evidence-responsive support; it does not itself establish a new official determination. Use the appropriate process rather than inventing a reclassification rule. [S2 source.obj0001.s2.2026-11-08; S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: FEL monitoring would have little purpose if status guaranteed success on every future academic task. Attend to actual academic progress and support needs. [S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08; S8 source.obj0001.s8.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: S7 anchors the monitoring period to reclassification and requires recognizing FELs at registration. Do not invent a fresh reclassification date or restart the clock on transfer. The four-year statement here is qualified to January 2026 guidance, retrieved 2026-11-08. [S7 source.obj0001.s7.2026-11-08; S8 source.obj0001.s8.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Avoid both disability misidentification and delay
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check. An EL's English proficiency is developing, and the school team also has a reason to suspect a disability. One colleague treats EL status as proof of disability; another wants to wait until English is mastered before considering evaluation. Which response reflects the still-linked February 2019 guidance's bounded principle?

options.text: Reject both shortcuts: EL status alone establishes neither disability nor a reason to delay evaluation when disability is suspected; use the appropriate team and evidence.
Prefer the first proposal, because difficulty learning English is enough to distinguish disability from language acquisition.
Prefer the second proposal, because evaluation can become relevant only after the student no longer has EL status.
Set aside the suspected disability whenever the student benefits from a language scaffold, because improvement resolves the question.

answerKey.feedback: The February 2019 guidance says EL status alone is not a basis for disability determination and should not delay a special education evaluation when disability is suspected. This is an older, still-linked source; the item teaches that principle only, not current IDEA timelines or a complete evaluation procedure. [S9 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: English proficiency alone cannot establish disability. The 2019 guidance explicitly warns against disability identification because of ELP. [S9 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: The same guidance rejects using EL status to delay evaluation where there is reason to suspect disability. Reclassification is not a prerequisite supplied by this excerpt. [S9 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Benefit from one scaffold does not remove the separately stated reason for suspecting disability. Do not substitute that classroom observation for the appropriate evaluation process or use EL status to delay it. [S9 source.obj0001.s9.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Unfamiliar transfer: a community archive project
tasks.prompt:
Original unfamiliar application in history/civics; not an official prompt. No deterministic answer key. Your reasoning remains pending review.

A class is designing an audio-and-text community archive about how a neighborhood public space has changed. Students must compare accounts, identify an uncertainty and justify an interpretation with evidence. All scenario information is synthetic.

Mara is newly enrolling without documented prior EL/FEL status. Her family's clarified Language Survey information fits a rubric scenario requiring an ELP screener, but no result is yet available. Section 2 requests translated messages. A colleague proposes immediate EL placement because Mara hesitated in an English interview.

Dev arrives with documented FEL status and an existing reclassification date. The school knows Dev remains within the monitoring period described by the January 2026 guidance, supplied retrieval 2026-11-08. Dev organizes historical images convincingly but has difficulty connecting the account and claim in writing. A staff member proposes restarting the monitoring period on registration.

Lin is an identified EL whose parent has voluntarily declined ELE services without reclassification. Lin can explain an interview source orally with help. A separate concern gives the team reason to suspect a disability. The scheduling group suggests treating opt-out as exit and waiting for English fluency before considering the disability concern. The history teacher also asks whether a vocabulary worksheet can count as ESL for students still receiving ESL.

Prepare a reasoned team plan with these connected parts:
1. For Mara, distinguish Section 1/protocol evidence, Section 2 family communication information and the interview observation. Explain the justified next step and what cannot yet be concluded. Name the determination/placement notification and record duties when decisions are made, without supplying deadlines or cut scores.
2. For Dev, explain how documented FEL status, academic observations and monitoring relate. Qualify any duration statement by the January 2026 guidance and supplied retrieval date. Address the proposed restart without inventing transfer procedures or annual schedules.
3. For Lin, distinguish service choice from status, annual English proficiency assessment and learning access. Address both disability shortcuts using the older February 2019 source's limited principle; do not invent evaluation timelines.
4. Design a short sequence for the archive task that preserves its historical reasoning goal, identifies an observable language goal, and explains content/ESL collaboration. Explain why a content scaffold cannot replace ESL, while acknowledging voluntary informed parent opt-out separately.
5. Write a concise evidence-sharing note that distinguishes content understanding, language use, assistance and unanswered questions. Justify your decisions with the relevant supplied sources and name at least one remaining policy-research gap.

Review focus: evidence-to-action reasoning, family access distinct from child identification, accurate notice/record scope, status versus service choice, qualified FEL continuity, shared instructional responsibility and the bounded disability principle. Several defensible instructional sequences are possible. Keyword matches, a copied model or completion of all parts do not establish an authoritative judgment, independence, transfer evidence or mastery. Source-checked refers only to model wording-to-source comparison, never human review of your response.

tasks.title: Keep population labels distinct and qualified
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A planning note says the June 2023 toolkit makes newcomer a universal three-year legal category, and each learner must fit exactly one of newcomer, refugee, SLIFE or LTEL. Which correction is supported?

options.text: Keep the three-year rule as a universal deadline, but allow refugee and newcomer to overlap.
Use refugee and SLIFE as interchangeable terms whenever prior schooling records are missing.
Qualify the toolkit definition by publisher/date; labels concern different aspects of experience, can overlap across a history, and do not supply an individual learning profile.
Replace the toolkit rule with the claim that every recently arrived learner meets Massachusetts SLIFE criteria.

answerKey.feedback: The June 2023 toolkit defines newcomer for its own purposes and calls the group heterogeneous. Labels may overlap but are not interchangeable; S4 requires specific MA SLIFE criteria. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08] NCELA’s November 2024 common LTEL duration usage concerns continuing EL status, not the June 2023 toolkit’s newcomer scope or a universal statutory cutoff. [S9 source.obj0002-0003.s9.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: The toolkit explicitly limits the definition to its own purposes. Its three-year wording is not a universal legal deadline for services or support. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Missing records or refugee experience alone do not establish the full June 2024 SLIFE criteria. The label cannot substitute for individual information. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Recent arrival does not establish DOE025 EL status, the age range, the enrollment/absence condition and the prior-schooling condition together. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Read all Massachusetts SLIFE conditions together
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A June 2024 MA SLIFE review has documented DOE025 EL status, age 15, and first U.S. school enrollment after grade 2. Information about prior formal schooling remains unclear. Which next statement is accurate?

options.text: The three known facts alone establish SLIFE; schooling history only affects the lesson plan.
Clarify the prior-schooling condition and use the district holistic support approach; the known facts alone do not establish all Exhibit 1 criteria.
Identify SLIFE only if a test first shows at least two years below grade expectations, regardless of schooling history.
Treat a family request for interpretation as the missing evidence of interrupted schooling.

answerKey.feedback: All Exhibit 1 conditions are conjunctive. Prior schooling must involve no formal schooling, significant interruptions or consistent but limited schooling, with holistic attention to significant support beyond existing ELE. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Exhibit 1 explicitly includes prior formal schooling as a condition. The other three conditions cannot replace it. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Approximately two or more years below appears among Exhibit 2 MAY characteristics, not as a required Exhibit 1 test cutoff. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: The required information concerns actual exposure to schooling. A family language preference does not establish that history. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Distinguish possible characteristics from required criteria
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A study guide says every student identified as SLIFE must function two or more years below grade level and that this establishes low ability. Which revision follows the primary June 2024 guidance?

options.text: Retain the two-years requirement, but remove the low-ability claim.
Remove all attention to literacy or schooling because assets mean support needs should not be discussed.
Use the FAQ sentence as the complete definition and assume its shorter wording supersedes Exhibit 1.
Treat the two-years feature as a possible characteristic, apply all Exhibit 1 criteria with holistic support, and avoid equating identification with ability or potential.

answerKey.feedback: Exhibit 2 uses MAY; Exhibit 1 supplies the required conditions. The guidance explicitly rejects a negative inference about ability or potential. Assets and support needs can both inform instruction. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Changing the ability language is necessary but incomplete: a possible Exhibit 2 characteristic still must not become a mandatory criterion. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: An asset perspective does not erase support needs. The guidance connects strengths and schooling information to support beyond existing ELE programs. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: The supplied packet identifies a compression conflict in the July 31, 2024 FAQ. Prefer the primary June 2024 Exhibit 1 and its full conditions, not the shorthand. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Interpret LTEL usage without a statutory cutoff
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A team uses an LTEL label for a secondary student with continuing EL status and proposes permanently removing demanding history work because “the label proves low ability.” What is the best response?

options.text: Examine the individual learning history and instructional access; NCELA describes common five-to-six-year usage, not an ESEA definition, and WIDA notes no standardized criteria.
Apply a universal five-year ESEA cutoff and conclude the student cannot benefit from grade-level content.
Ignore the student’s actual progress because no standardized label means no instructional question exists.
Assume motivation is the cause whenever a student remains an EL beyond six years.

answerKey.feedback: The November 2024 fact sheet explicitly says LTEL is not defined in ESEA and asks about program fit and access. WIDA, February 2, 2026, notes no standardized criteria and emphasizes individual stories and authentic opportunities. [S10 source.obj0002-0003.s10.2026-11-08] [S9 source.obj0002-0003.s9.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: Common five-to-six-year usage is not a universal ESEA cutoff or an ability measure. The source warns of inequitable content access. [S9 source.obj0002-0003.s9.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: No standardized duration criteria does not erase the need to understand the learner and ensure authentic learning opportunities. [S10 source.obj0002-0003.s10.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Continuing status alone does not establish motivation or cause. Program and instructional fit may need attention; investigate actual strengths and needs. [S9 source.obj0002-0003.s9.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Preserve a reasoning goal while responding to schooling assets
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. Two newcomers are comparing evidence for competing habitat claims. One has extensive prior literacy and science schooling; the other explains local observations orally but is unfamiliar with written-source routines after schooling interruptions. Which plan best preserves the goal?

options.text: Give both a copying task because a newcomer label determines the appropriate cognitive level.
Remove the comparison goal until both can write fluent English paragraphs without help.
Keep evidence comparison for both, connect the first learner’s literacy to English explanation, model written-source routines with oral rehearsal for the second, and observe each response.
Value the second learner’s oral knowledge but assign only everyday conversation practice until formal literacy develops enough for evidence reasoning.

answerKey.feedback: Heterogeneity and assets justify observing individual access needs while preserving meaningful learning. These particular scaffolds are authored possibilities, not mandated methods. SLIFE assets and varying literacy do not imply low ability. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08] [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: A group label does not establish one cognitive level or support plan; copying also removes the stated reasoning goal. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Supporting cultural and linguistic assets can help access the meaningful task while English develops; fluent unsupported writing is not a prerequisite supplied by this source. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Observed oral knowledge and lived expertise can support reasoning now. Interrupted schooling and emerging literacy do not establish an absence of capacity; provide access to the evidence task while developing literacy. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Make support accessible without diagnosing trauma
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A newcomer is quiet during a class presentation. A colleague proposes repeated interviews about possible traumatic events before offering any classroom support. What should change?

options.text: Diagnose trauma from silence and tell every teacher the family’s complete migration story.
Offer predictable access supports, privately clarify present needs, share only essential support information through appropriate processes, and avoid requiring repeated sensitive retelling.
Make a whole-class personal journey story a required first step to build empathy before offering classroom supports.
Rule out all emotional needs because no trauma has been disclosed.

answerKey.feedback: The guidance supports privacy and avoiding repeated recounting of sensitive experiences. Emotional needs vary; a quiet observation neither diagnoses trauma nor rules needs out. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08] [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Silence is not a diagnosis. Heterogeneous needs require individual attention; the label or one behavior does not establish trauma. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: An empathy-building intention does not justify required sensitive disclosure or making support depend on a personal story. Protect privacy and avoid requiring students to recount potentially sensitive experiences. [S4 source.obj0002-0003.s4.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Lack of disclosure does not establish lack of need. Make support accessible and respond to observations without a clinical inference. [S8 source.obj0002-0003.s8.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Investigate educational expectations without national typing
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A student waits for a teacher demonstration before trying a new task. A staff member says the student’s nationality proves a fixed deductive learning style. Which response is strongest?

options.text: Keep the national label and permanently restrict the student to teacher demonstrations.
Treat the wait as proof that the student lacks the ability to discover patterns.
Assume culture can never affect expectations, so avoid asking about prior classroom routines.
Describe the observed wait, explain and model the new routine, ask about prior opportunities and observe responses across approaches without assigning a national learning type.

answerKey.feedback: Statement 0002.ds.04 supports awareness of culturally influenced educational practices. It does not justify assigning a fixed learning style from nationality; inquiry and response to observed opportunities are authored applications. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.a: Awareness of possible educational differences does not establish one permanent type for a nationality or justify restricting opportunity. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.b: Waiting in one task provides no ability conclusion. The framework asks about practices and effects on learning, not diagnosis from a single behavior. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: The statement explicitly includes culturally influenced educational practices. Consider possibilities respectfully without treating culture as either irrelevant or a deterministic explanation. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Use deep/surface culture as inquiry
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. A school adds a food display but leaves an unexplained fast-paced discussion routine that excludes some learners. Which revision uses the framework’s culture concepts responsibly?

options.text: Keep welcoming contributions and investigate participation expectations, explain routines and invite individual feedback without inferring a nationality’s cultural type.
Declare the display sufficient because culture consists only of food and celebrations.
Assign each national group a collectivist or individualist profile and set participation roles from that profile.
Label every hesitant learner as experiencing culture shock and remove them from discussion.

answerKey.feedback: The framework includes deep/surface culture, communication patterns and cultural adaptation. The authored application is to investigate expectations as well as visible traditions without stereotyping or diagnosing adjustment. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]

wrongFeedback.b: The statement extends beyond surface examples to assumptions, beliefs, values and communication patterns; a display alone does not address the stated participation barrier. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.c: Collectivism/individualism are conceptual tools for awareness, not instructions to assign uniform national types or roles. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]
wrongFeedback.d: Mentioning cultural adaptation does not make hesitation a diagnosis of culture shock. Investigate access and individual circumstances before drawing conclusions. [S1 source.obj0002-0003.s1.2026-11-08]

tasks.title: Use family languages as learning resources
tasks.prompt: Original unaided check; synthetic illustrative practice. Students are comparing explanations of a community place. A caregiver offers an oral account in a familiar language and agrees to its use. Which response best uses the contribution for learning?

options.text: Require an English essay before the account can count as knowledge.
Use an accessible, competently supported account as one source students compare with another, and invite the caregiver’s perspective without treating it as representative of every family.
Display a greeting in that language but exclude the account from the reasoning task.
